main.title: The pinhole
main.question: How can a hole make a picture?

transcript.text: Before you put the lens into your camera, try something.
Leave the lens out, and drop this in instead:
a thin metal disc with one tiny hole in it, a quarter of a millimetre across.
That's it.
No glass, and nothing that could focus anything.
And yet, if you open the shutter, count,
and close it again, there's a photograph on the film.
So how does a hole make a picture?
Ask people that, and most of them say the same thing:
the hole must work like a tiny lens, bending the light into focus.
It's a reasonable guess.
It's also wrong.
Because a hole isn't a thing.
It's a gap.
There's no glass in there, so there's nothing that could bend light at all.
So if the hole isn't bending the light, what is it doing?
Start with no camera at all.
Picture a tree on a sunny day,
and a sheet of film just sitting out in the open, facing it.
Every point on that tree is scattering sunlight in every direction at once.
So the light from the very top of the tree lands all over the film.
And the light from the very bottom?
That lands all over the film too.
Every spot on the film is getting light from every part of the tree,
all piled up together.
Add it all up, and you just get an even glow.
So the picture isn't missing.
All the light you'd need for it is right there.
It's just hopelessly mixed up.
Now put a wall between the tree and the film, with one small hole in it.
Before I show you, decide: what does the film see now?
Start at the top of the tree.
The wall stops every ray from up there,
except the one that happens to line up with the hole.
That one sails straight through, and lands low on the film.
It's the same story at the bottom of the tree: one ray makes it through,
and because it's heading upwards, it lands up high.
So now every part of the tree gets its own private spot on the film,
and that is exactly what a picture is.
It's upside down, because all the rays cross over at the hole.
And notice what the hole actually did there.
It didn't add anything.
It threw away almost all of the light, and whatever survived was already sorted.
How would you check that?
About a thousand years ago, a scholar called Ibn al-Haytham did exactly that.
He lined up several lamps in front of one small opening, with a dark room behind it.
Your turn again.
If light really does go straight through that opening,
how many spots of light show up on the far wall, and in what order?
You get one spot for every lamp, in the opposite order.
And if you cover up just one lamp, just one spot goes dark: its own.
So each lamp's light is keeping to its own straight line.
Nothing's getting mixed, and nothing's getting bent.
So if a hole is all you need, why does any camera bother with a lens?
Because there's a catch.
Say you make the hole bigger.
More light gets in.
But now every point of the tree paints a blob instead of a dot, and the blobs overlap.
So the picture gets brighter, and blurrier.
So go the other way.
Make the hole smaller, and the picture gets sharper, but only up to a point.
Because if you send light through a small enough hole,
it starts to spread out on the far side, and the picture goes soft all over again.
So somewhere in between there's a best size,
and for this camera it works out at 0.24 millimetres.
The disc in your kit is drilled at 0.25.
But that sharpness costs you something.
The smallest opening your camera's lens ever uses is about two millimetres across,
and next to that, the pinhole lets in sixty-seven times less light.
Which is why you don't click the shutter with a pinhole.
You open it, and you count.
In full sun, it's just open, shut.
In the shade, count to three.
And indoors by a window, you're counting all the way to forty.
A hole doesn't bend light.
It sorts it.
That's the pinhole experiment in your kit:
two pictures on your roll, made with nothing but a hole.
But it leaves you stuck with a problem.
A sharp picture needs a small hole, and a small hole is dim.
A bright picture needs a big hole, and a big hole is blurry.
What if you could keep the big, bright opening, and still get the sharp picture?
That's exactly the job of the piece you left out at the start: the lens.
And that's the next lesson.

But fingers aren't alike.
A slow press and a quick press would give you two different pictures.
And this camera hasn't got a strong spring.
The real answer is a click.
To see why it matters, go back to 1839, when a picture took minutes.
The shutter was a cap.
You took it off, you counted, you put it back.
In lesson one you did the same job yourself: open, count, close.
Then plates got faster, and suddenly no hand was quick enough.
In June 1878, Eadweard Muybridge set up twelve cameras beside a racetrack,

As the horses ran past, they broke the wires, and each wire fired one camera's shutter.

By the 1880s, a simple fast shutter was just a plate with a hole in it,

Yours is the same idea, swung instead of dropped.
The blade turns on a peg, and it has one window.
At rest, solid plastic covers the lens.
Press, and the blade swings across.

One press, one picture.

main.title: Light traps
main.question: How can a box full of gaps be dark inside?

transcript.text: Two winders that turn, a frame wheel that spins, a back that comes right off.
This thing is full of gaps.
And inside it is film that a single moment of daylight would ruin.
So how can a box full of gaps be dark inside?
Most people guess that it must be sealed, like a jar with its lid on.
It isn't sealed anywhere.
Each winder has over half a millimetre of room around it, so that it can turn.
The back sits in its groove with room to spare.
Air could get through every one of those gaps.
But here's the difference: air goes round corners.
Light, mostly, doesn't.
And that is the whole trick.
You've met this idea before.
Light travels in straight lines.
About a thousand years ago, Ibn al-Haytham showed it with his lamps and one opening:
screen one lamp, and only its spot goes out.
Each spot had come straight from its own lamp.
So a gap is harmless, as long as no straight line runs through it to the film.
Here's the joint where the back meets the body, cut through so you can see it.
A ridge on the back stands in a groove in the body, with a step on each side.
Any light coming in has to turn one corner, then another, then another.
The ridge reaches almost two millimetres in,
so even a back that's been left a little open has no straight way in.
The winders do the same thing.
Each head lies flat on the top of the body.
A ring on the stem runs in a channel, and a block on the back closes the slot behind it.
Even the film's own shell keeps itself dark this way.
In 1934, film started coming in a metal shell you could load in daylight,
and its slot is lined with soft fibres.
Now, how do you check a camera that nobody has printed yet?
You fire light at the computer model.
You run it backwards.
Rays leave the film in every direction, because a way out is also a way in.
Twenty-one cases: the shutter loose or pushed, a thin print, the frame wheel up and down.
Sixty-nine million rays.
Not one of them reached the outside.
But does the test even work?
Hold the shutter open, and 251 rays escape,
and every one of them leaves through the lens's opening,
exactly where light is meant to come in.
So the test can find light.
With the shutter shut, it found none.
Straight lines are only half the story, though.
Light also bounces, and no plastic is perfectly black.
So here's a sum.
The model lets every surface send back 30 percent of the light,
which is more than black plastic really does.
One bounce keeps 0.3.
Two bounces: 0.3 times 0.3, which is 0.09.
Three bounces: 0.027, about one part in 37.
Five bounces: about one part in 400.
And most bounced light heads off the wrong way anyway.
Every corner divides the light again.
That's why it's called a light trap.
In your kit, press the back on until both ends click.
A back left standing off is the biggest risk to your pictures.
The parts that keep the light out are printed black,
and the shape does the rest: every gap is a light trap.
And open the back only when the film is wound home into its shell.
So is it proved?
Not yet.
Rays in a computer are not light on film.
The real test waits for a printed camera:
a loaded roll, the lens covered, an hour in the sun.
If a frame comes back fogged, the shape of the fog will point to the gap.
So how can a box full of gaps be dark?
No straight line runs through any gap, and every bounce throws light away.
You can find one tonight.
In a dark room, look for where light shows round a closed door,
and ask yourself where the gap runs straight.
And try this: make a light trap from a shoebox and some card, and test it with a torch.
So now the camera gathers light, measures it out, moves the film and keeps the dark in.
All of that is the camera's job.
The last part is yours.
Next time: same camera, same film, so why are some pictures better than others?
Every ray here was drawn in the computer.
Nothing has been printed, and no photograph has been taken.

main.title: Aiming and framing
main.question: Same camera, same film. Why are some pictures better than others?

render.alt: The camera from the front with the handle set at a dot

main.hook: Two people, the same camera, the same roll, the same afternoon. One comes home with pictures people stop to look at. This camera has one speed, three dots and nothing to focus, so it isn't the camera. It's four choices: where you aim, where you stand, where the light comes from, and how still you hold.

xref.idea: With one speed, three dots and fixed focus, a good picture is choices: the light, the distance, the middle of the frame.

facts.sentence: Stand two big steps (2 m) or more from what you photograph; nearer is soft because the focus is fixed.
ISO 400 film in full sun, hard shadows: the small dot.

main.title: Your phone's camera
main.question: Your phone has no film, no dots and no blade. So how does it take a picture?
main.hook: Open your phone's camera and every piece of the CURVE 35 is in there, shrunk to the size of a pea: the dark box, the hole, the lens, the shutter, the thing that catches light. They just work differently. Here they all are again, and the one idea that ties them together.

xref.idea: A phone camera has every piece of this one: dark box, hole, lens, shutter and something that remembers light.
